FreeBSD Core Team The FreeBSD Core Team is the governing body of FreeBSD. Completed items We completed the following items: Handover from the previous Core Team The handover from core.13 was completed: mail aliases, the LDAP group, and the Phabricator group now contain only core.14 members. Core liaisons FreeBSD Foundation: bapt@ (with most of core@ participating in monthly Foundation meetings) secteam: kevans@ clusteradm: adrian@ srcmgr: imp@ portmgr: adamw@, olivier@ doceng: hrs@ re: hrs@ Public meeting minutes We reached consensus to publish our public meeting minutes, which were previously only sent to the developers mailing list. FreeBSD Developer AI survey bapt@ created a survey for FreeBSD developers on the use of AI and LLMs. He presented the results to core@, and a summary was shared with developers. 140 developers responded. Policy: 88% want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49%) or light guidance and best practices (39%). 6% said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and 3% that the existing contribution rules are sufficient. AI-assisted code: 35% said it must be disclosed, 25% that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22% that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16% that it should be rejected outright. Safeguards: mandatory human review (78%) and mandatory disclosure (69%) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47%) and mandatory testing (39%). Disclosure: 84% want AI use disclosed, either always (48%) or when its involvement is significant (36%). 79% want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56% prefer a tag that names the tool. Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39%), licensing and provenance (26%), and maintainability (21%). 75% are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing. Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91%), and transparency (78%) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy. Other uses: 65% would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54% would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29% would not. The FreeBSD Foundation asked for a core representative on the committee for the upcoming user survey. jrm@ volunteered. Ports repository freeze and history rewrite On 2026-07-20, a 150 MB binary file was mistakenly committed to the ports tree. The commit broke mirroring to GitHub, which rejects files larger than 100 MB, and added a file of questionable licensing to the repository history. On 2026-07-21, core@ decided to freeze the ports repository to limit the number of commits that would need to be rewritten, and worked out a plan with clusteradm@, portmgr@, and the Git administrators. kevans@ published a signed statement on 2026-07-22 to explain the freeze and to make clear that the ports tree had not been compromised. The offending commits were removed by rewriting the history of the main branch, and package builds from the old hashes were stopped. New server-side hooks now guard against a recurrence. EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) statement The FreeBSD Foundation asked core@ to recognize it as an open source steward. We settled on a statement of support, which was published on the announce and developers mailing lists. Releases We reviewed the draft announcement for 14.5-RELEASE and the proposed schedule for 15.2-RELEASE. Developer and contributor conflicts We dealt with conflicts between developers and external contributors. Decisions were communicated to the parties involved. Correspondence We handled correspondence on a number of topics, including the current and future AI policy work and the impact of increased AI/bot-driven scraping on FreeBSD infrastructure. Work in progress Core secretary role We are defining the scope of a funded secretary role, which may serve the whole project rather than only core@. Examples from other non-profits and FreeBSD working groups are being used as a reference. There is rough consensus to move the role towards a project management assistant. A proposal was shared with the FreeBSD Foundation and feedback is pending. AI policy imp@ created an AI working group made up of people with diverse opinions on the topic. The working group will use the developer survey results as input for a policy on the use of AI/LLMs. The kickoff meeting of the group will be held on October 7. Final reports are expected in Q4. Bylaws and core terms We are continuing the previous Core Team’s work on staggered terms. We consider ourselves a transitional Core Team and plan to invoke the bylaws' staggering provision, with the change taking effect in 2027. Before the 2027 election, we will designate which members step down after one year and which serve a full two-year term; the vacated seats will be filled in that election. Regularizing policy Efforts are underway to modernize and centralize the FreeBSD Project’s policy documentation, which is currently inconsistent, poorly visible, and reliant on unwritten "tribal knowledge." imp@ is working to consolidate existing guidelines, resolve policy contradictions between project groups, and formally record long-standing traditions. Additionally, this initiative will identify gaps where new, formal policies are needed to ensure smooth, efficient operations. We hope to have this wrapped up by the end of Q1 2027. Liaison expectations We are documenting the responsibilities of each liaison role and will publish the document once it is complete. Workflow organization We are evaluating tooling to track our tasks, documents, and correspondence. We began using a CryptPad instance set up by bapt@ and clusteradm@. Policy on reasonable content for Project spaces We discussed writing down the Project norms for what content is reasonable for Project spaces, such as the wiki and repository metadata. Over the years, we have developed a tradition of avoiding politics, religion, and other contentious issues unrelated to the Project, and need to write it down and bring it in line with open source norms. portmgr structure We are discussing the structure of portmgr@ and how to revamp the team. Cluster administration planning adrian@ and some clusteradm@ members are preparing a budget, prioritizing work, improving documentation and processes, and planning to recruit new team members in 2027. Returning developers srcmgr@ has a new policy for returning developers, which asks for some recent work or plans before access is restored, and portmgr@ has something similar. We are discussing whether it makes sense for these policies to be aligned across teams. Privacy requests core@ received a GDPR erasure request covering mailing list posts from more than twenty years ago. Removing content from public mailing list archives is not practical, especially for archives the Project does not control. The Project has a privacy policy, which should be extended to cover mailing lists, Bugzilla, and other services. We communicated this to the person requesting the removal. Core and FreeBSD Foundation meetings Monthly meetings are scheduled through December 2026. Bay Area Vendor Summit in November We are planning a short introduction and update followed by a question and answer session. FreeBSD Foundation The FreeBSD Foundation is a 501(c)(3) non-profit dedicated to advancing FreeBSD through both technical and non-technical support. Funded entirely by donations, the Foundation supports software development, infrastructure, security, and collaboration efforts; organizes events and developer summits; provides educational resources; and represents the FreeBSD Project in legal matters. Advocacy In the third quarter of 2026, our advocacy efforts focused on expanding our educational video content, engaging with the FreeBSD community, and preparing for the upcoming FreeBSD Vendor Summit. We also continued highlighting the people, projects, and initiatives that support FreeBSD’s growth and long-term success. Sponsor: The FreeBSD Foundation x11appjail: Tool for creating, verifying, installing, and running AppJails x11appjail is a specialized tool for creating, verifying, installing, and running AppJails. An AppJail is a CLI, TUI or X11 application that runs inside a FreeBSD jail but is perceived by the end user as identical (or at least very similar) to an application running directly on the host system. This tool makes extensive use of appjail(1) as its engine; however, unlike the latter, the primary user in x11appjail is neither root nor a privileged user, but rather an unprivileged user. The fundamental goal of this project is to grant the user limited access to the jail, restricted solely to the execution of a CLI, TUI or X11 application. This project began months ago as a prototype to establish a workflow leveraging appjail-x11(1); however, starting with version 1.0.0, it was rewritten from scratch into a unified tool that integrates all its projects, such as sysutils/appjail, sysutils/unixexec, archivers/appscript, and sysutils/jtransfer, among others. Even better, it allows for the execution of not only X11 applications but also CLI and TUI programs. The most relevant project for x11appjail(1) is not only appjail(1), but also appscript(1). My goal with appscript(1) is to create an ultra-lightweight alternative to AppImage for FreeBSD that does not depend on FUSE, thus eliminating the need to configure vfs.usermount=1. appscript(1) allows you to create an elf(5) executable that contains everything necessary to run a self-contained executable. Executables created by appscript(1) extract the payload cooperatively: the leader process extracts the payload once using an exclusive lock, while other processes (if any) wait using a shared lock. Unlike previous versions, where the payload was extracted to a random directory upon every execution, this significantly improves performance by extracting the payload only once; furthermore, the resulting directory is removed by the last remaining process once no running processes remain. appscript-verify(1) is a new command installed by archivers/appscript to verify executables signed with signify(1); it is particularly relevant to x11appjail(1)'s veriexec (see below). x11appjail(1)'s veriexec is an internal tool used by x11appjail(1) to run an AppJail in portable mode only if it is signed with a trusted key. This tool is unrelated to NetBSD’s veriexec. Both tools support the classic, battle-tested SHA-256 algorithm and the faster yet secure BLAKE3 algorithm. When sysutils/b3sum is available (the default if x11appjail(1) was installed from ports), BLAKE3 is the default choice, unless SHA-256 is explicitly specified in rc.conf(5). The checksum algorithm is fundamental to both x11appjail(1) and appscript(1). In the case of x11appjail(1), the algorithm is used in internal operations such as veriexec, whereas appscript(1) uses it to verify executables. BLAKE3 has been selected as the default option because it offers greater speed without compromising security. Attributes have been implemented in x11appjail(1) as a means for both the user and the system operator to manipulate the behavior of an AppJail. For example, a system operator can create the system attribute users.uid.perms, the content of which might be "enable_3d sound usb webcam". An unprivileged user can create the user attributes appname:profile.allow.enable_3d and appname:profile.allow.sound. Subsequently, when executing an AppJail, devices become visible or remain hidden depending on whether the user holds the corresponding permission and has authorized those permissions for the jail being created. In this case, the hardware acceleration and sound devices will become visible, provided the AppJail has incorporated the necessary logic to make them visible. Another notable change worth mentioning for x11appjail(1) are the examples added in ${EXAMPLESDIR}/Apps: badwolf, chromium, evince, feh, firefox, htop, linux-brave, mpv, nanonote, telegram-desktop and thunderbird. Beyond the applications themselves, the key factor is the deployment method. htop is an example of a CLI application, linux-brave is a Linux application, and the others are X11 applications. Web browsers, Mpv, and Thunderbird are the most interesting examples, as they demonstrate how an AppJail can use VirtualGL to properly enable hardware acceleration within a FreeBSD jail, something that would not normally be possible given that Xephyr is the backend used by appjail-x11(1). Best of all, from the end-user’s perspective, all of this is transparent. Port of rdma-core project to FreeBSD The Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) infrastructure provides high-performance interconnect between computing and storage nodes. It can operate over different physical networks, for instance Ethernet and Infiniband. The implementation of the RDMA stack consists of several components. There is the core kernel infrastructure, and drivers for Host Channel Adapters (HCAs), providing access to the kernel verbs. Userspace applications never interact with the kernel devices directly, the core libibverbs library and vendor-specific userspace drivers provide unified and device-specific verbs. Since RDMA intent of providing low-latency low-overhead operations, performant HCAs offload a lot of operations from CPU. Also, typical in-line operations like send and receive can be initiated and completed in userspace, where kernel only assists in the connection establishment and teardown. Due to this, the userspace RDMA software stack is crucial for its operations. FreeBSD base system includes port of the so called OFED kernel core component, kernel drivers, as well as userspace core (libibverbs) and userspace drivers, for instance libmlx5 for managing Nvidia Connect-X4 and later HCAs. Over time, the kernel parts get some significant updates from the infiniband code in the Linux kernel, which become the home for updated OFED. Userspace part of OFED was converted into the rdma-core userspace project, that only supports Linux (and glibc). Since userspace drivers in rdma-core provide essential functionality, and since FreeBSD userspace RDMA components are quite outdated, the situation overall needs a resolution. We attempted to update the in-tree userspace components by importing the series of rdma-core commits with dependencies, but it quickly proved to be not feasible. Instead we started looking at what it would take to make rdma-core compile and run on FreeBSD. First, there were a number of missing glibc-specific APIs that were used in rdma-core, for instance, strdupa() and friends, main:tdestroy(3), some pthread functions. These were easy to handle in the base system, and addition of them benefited the whole FreeBSD porting story. Next, and more serious, the unportable features of glibc were used everywhere in the sources, and trying to cover them all would cause huge porting patch, which is problematic to push upstream, even for cooperating upstream. Instead, the idea of using an approach similar to LinuxKPI for kernel code, was formed and developed, called LinuxAPI. Unlike LinuxKPI, which handles architectural mismatches between Linux kernel and FreeBSD kernel, in addition to the different C interfaces, LinuxAPI needs to smooth out the differences around extensions to the same core functionality defined by POSIX. It is mostly about bits that are not defined by POSIX but needed for RDMA to function, like networking interface enumeration, or discovery of the rdma-capable devices and their capabilities etc. It seems that people consider the LinuxAPI useful outside the rdma-core porting efforts already, there is a project github.com/freebsd/linuxapi which takes the developed set of headers and extends it further. We are currently working on providing the permissive license to make the library useful without additional strings attached. Our initial goal, also limited by the available hardware, is to have rdma-core work with the ConnectX-4 cards. Of course we welcome all vendors interested in RDMA on FreeBSD to improve the port to properly support their cards. The result of the porting is available as the repository. Sponsor: The FreeBSD Foundation Procdesc: debugging API The process descriptors API enhancements project continued, with the goal to allow complete process control using descriptors, in particular, debugging. I wanted to make it possible to stop reference pids as the process identifiers. The milestone for it should be a demonstration of enabling the capsicum mode for some non-trivial debugger, I selected truss(1) because it does not need neither filesystem nor network namespace accesses after attached to the target. The semi-obvious solution there is to introduce pdptrace(2), which is equivalent to ptrace(2) but takes the process descriptor as the process designator. We need to be able to obtain the notifications of the process debugging events, which are provided by waitpid[2] syscall family for pid-based controls. And, we need a way to obtain the process descriptor for a new child forked from the debuggee, to continue tracing of all descendants. Previously, the pdopenpid(2) system call was added, which allows to get a handle on an arbitrary process. Existing operations on the process descriptors are somewhat limited: handle owner can wait for the exit notification using kqueue(2), and with some luck retrieve the process exit status. The last point requires some elaboration. Since the pdwait(2) call was added recently, there were some amount of hacks in the kernel to allow waitpid(2) calls on pid’s of processes created with pdfork(2). As result, the waitpid(2) caller might have reaped the process before owner of the process descriptor could call pdwait(2). Similarly, if there is more than one process descriptor opened on the same process, only the first pdwait(2) caller could retrieve the exit status with pdwait(2), making other descriptors useless. The listed set of problems also made it very hard to correctly use the proposed pdptrace(2). The process being debugged could steal events from process descriptors and vice versa. Simply disallowing wait(2) on processes with the opened descriptors is not an option for two reasons: * backward compatibility, waitpid(2) was already allowed and existing binaries relied on it * if the debuggee used fork(2) to create a child, it expects to get the exit notification (e.g. SIGCHLD) and exit status from wait(2) The solution was manyfold. First, we have to postpone reaping if there are either opened process descriptors, or if the process was created with fork(2), we should not reap until wait(2) is called on pid by the parent. Second, the exit status needs to be preserved in the process descriptors private data even after reaping, to allow pdwait(2) on any of the descriptors. This was implemented by providing a bitmap of the 'zombie refs' on the kernel struct proc. Each zombie reference prevents reaping, and cleared by corresponding call to waitpid(2) or pdwait(2). Only when all registered references are cleared, zombie can be reaped. If the process is created with pdfork(2) or opened with pdopenpid[2], it gets the procdesc zombie reference. If the process was created with fork(2), it gets the 'parent' zombie reference. By default, pdfork[2] also sets the parent reference to allow the waitpid(2), for compatibility. The new pdfork(2) flag PD_NOWAITPID prevents that. Then, wait-like events must work with the process descriptors. The procdesc kqueue(2) event filter was extended with NOTE_PDSIGCHLD hints to report that pdwait(2) can retrieve tracing or exiting event on the descriptor. Then, the pdptrace(2) was able to usefully control the target. A new ptrace call to retrieve the list of the attached processes PT_GET_CHILDREN allowed pdptrace(2) to get hold of forks. With all the features implemented, it was possible to convert truss(1) to use only process descriptors to control the traced processes. The existing mode of using pids was preserved, and can be selected with the '-y' option as an emergency switch and to easy comparison and debugging of the new mode. Until this quarter it reported every call, which for anything larger than a toy program buries the calls of interest. HEAD now accepts -t with a comma-separated expression naming the system calls to report. The option letter is the one System V Release 4 and SunOS truss use for this. A term may be a system call name, an fnmatch(3) glob (readlink*), a system call number in the traced process’s ABI, or @group for a family of related calls. Terms apply in order; the last match wins. truss -t with no expression lists the groups and exits. Groups are themselves -t expressions, so they compose without a second language. @desc is built from @read and @write rather than repeating their members. Member lists are patterns (extattr_*file, sctp*) rather than frozen name lists, so a later system call that follows the same naming convention joins the right group without a source change here. Sponsor: Netflix x86 splitlocks detection support Most non-x86 platforms are relatively strict with regard to the proper alignment of the data types. On the other hand, x86 ISA allows any alignment for the operands of integer scalar operations. Still, there is an AC control bit in the processor flags register which causes alignment exception (fault) on unaligned operations. Practically the bit is not too useful because most of the compilers generate code that relies on the freedom of the working unaligned access on x86. Particularly interesting case of the unaligned access is when the disposition of the operand causes it to span two cache lines (which is impossible for naturally aligned data). Normal (unlocked) operations cause so called torn reads and writes. This effect become observable starting with Core2 Intel microarchitecture. Even more interesting case is provided by the locked operations using the LOCK prefix on read-modify-write instruction with the mis-aligned data. To satisfy ISA guarantees in this case, the CPU has to either take more than one cache line for exclusive ownership in MESI-like cache coherence protocol, or exercise so called bus lock ensuring global cache ownership. Either option has very high cost and causes observable detrimental effects on other processes and virtual machines executing on the same physical host. Since some time Intel provides a control for the lock operations that need to span more than one cache line (split locks). Turning the control on causes split locks to generate the same #AC exception as done by the AC flag, but only for the split locks, instead of all unaligned accesses. The feature is controlled by the platform MSR and is per-CPU global, which precludes making the MSR directly available to userspace. The new sysarch(2) operation I386_SET_SPLITLOCK was developed that enables the control for the calling thread. The control is part of the machine state maintained on the context switch. The intent is mainly to assist in catching bugs where improperly alignment locking structures are created, unlike Linux, which uses the feature to artificially penalize such processes by slowing them down. If the program code modifications are not possible, users and administrators can LD_PRELOAD a trivial shared object that turns the control on. The step daemon acquires reaper status, tracks descendants across process-group changes and nested reapers, and signals the tracked process tree during cleanup. On a FreeBSD test node it cleaned up orphaned, SIGTERM-resistant and nested children like proctrack/pgid, and additionally handled setsid, setpgid, double-fork and nested-daemon escapes, which proctrack/pgid does not. A zombie regression was retested and the node returned to IDLE without timing out or draining. Submitted %o support for Include filenames in Slurm configuration to SchedMD. Include slurm-%o.conf selects slurm-FreeBSD.conf on FreeBSD and slurm-Linux.conf on Linux, so a heterogeneous configless cluster can keep one authoritative configuration on slurmctld. This has been running on a mixed FreeBSD/Fedora cluster using the corresponding port patches.
